analysis.one_liner: Abolishes the federal agency that sets and enforces workplace safety standards.
analysis.headline: The bill to abolish OSHA was referred to committee, never received a hearing or a vote, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have repealed the 1970 law that created OSHA and shut the agency down, eliminating the federal workplace safety and health standards, inspections, enforcement, and training that OSHA provides [S2][S3]. It was introduced by Rep. Andy Biggs with three cosponsors among the bill's original backers and a total of 9 Republican cosponsors, referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, and never moved again [S1][S4][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, particularly those in hazardous industries, would gain because federal safety standards, inspections, and penalties would disappear. Workers would bear the cost in the form of weaker protection from workplace injury, illness, and death.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Occupational Safety and Health Act of 1970 and abolishes OSHA, removing federal workplace safety standard-setting, enforcement, inspections, and penalties.
Its beneficiaries would be employers, who would no longer face federal safety rules, inspections, or citations.

analysis.who_pays: Workers, who would lose the federal safety standards, inspections, and enforcement that protect them from workplace hazards.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the OSH Act would eliminate the federal agency that sets and enforces workplace safety standards, removing national minimum protections against unsafe working conditions.
Workers in states that do not run their own federally approved safety programs, and workers whose state protections are weaker, would have no federal floor of workplace safety protection.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill never advanced, so there was no real-world cost or benefit. Had it passed, workers would have lost the main federal backstop against unsafe workplaces, with the gain accruing to employers who would face no federal safety inspections, enforcement, or penalties. The strongest argument for the bill—that federal rules can overburden small businesses—was never weighed against the loss of the federal guarantee of safe working conditions.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, got no further action, and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Biggs introduced the NOSHA Act on November 2, 2021, to repeal the OSH Act of 1970 and abolish OSHA.
The House referred the bill to the Education and Labor Committee the same day; no further action was ever taken.
The bill never received a hearing, a markup, a floor vote, or cosponsors from the majority party, and expired with the Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers kept federal workplace safety protections. Employers who would have benefited from abolishing OSHA gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Andy Biggs
for.what_they_did: Introduced the NOSHA Act to repeal the OSH Act of 1970 and abolish OSHA.

for.name: Reps. Chip Roy, Thomas Massie, and Matt Gaetz
for.role: U.S. Representatives (R-TX, R-KY, R-FL), original cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

sides.party_line_note: All 9 cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill sat in a House committee controlled by the Democratic majority, which took no action on it [S4][S5].

industries.note: Abolishing OSHA would remove federal safety standards, inspections, and the threat of citations and penalties. The cost of workplace injuries would shift largely to workers themselves.
Workers would lose the federal agency responsible for workplace safety standards and enforcement, leaving them with fewer protections against injury on the job.
